chapter: Youth and day jobs in New Orleans
title: Day jobs: coal wagon alongside Louis Armstrong and long-shore work
summary: Foster and Louis both drove coal wagons; he held several day jobs while playing every night.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: And I did all kind of work in my life. See, I used to, so for me and Louis both drove coal wagon. He drove coal wagon, Louis Armstrong. See, he ever said that when he drove coal wagon?

So you told me about that. Well, Tennessee coal company and I waited for the Pittsburgh coal company. See. And we used to meet. I'd buy her the whisker. See, I was for uptown coal company. But I'd be delivering coal downtown and he's coming uptown to us. So we'll meet over here and we'll wait. This morning it was my boy and the morning it was his boy. Yeah. Ten cents a supper and best whisker. Get that pop. The bottle would just send a pop in the back of his, we call it pop. It was better and bigger. Get a pop bottle, get ten cents of the Vigarees, go to a place called Vigarees. Get a man ten cents and go to the bottle of Philippi whiskey with it. See. Then I drove Duncourt Hall, fill up lots. And I was married. I'd have to take care of my mother, send us to school. Then I'd drive the Longshorns. And I'd wait for Longshorns. And I'd play every night. I'd work pretty hard in my young days. And I had some of the best jobs. I've been a bass player in New York. Had some of the best jobs of any of the bass players. See. Well, I was going to ask a little bit about the whole rhythm section, like the drummers that you've worked with and you talking about how the drummers play today compared to… Well, there ain't no drummers today. They're cymbal beaters. You put that on there. Yeah, that's… They're cymbal beaters.
